title: Amrecibart and cenvacibart for the prevention of catheter-related thrombosis (ROXI-CATH): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are often complicated by venous thromboembolism, yet no thromboprophylaxis is approved. Factor XI (FXI) inhibition might prevent catheter-associated venous thromboembolism without increasing bleeding. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of amrecibart and cenvacibart for preventing venous thromboembolism after PICC placement. METHODS: ROXI-CATH is a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial conducted across 12 hospital centres in Bulgaria, Canada, Israel, Romania, the UK, and the USA. Eligible participants aged 18 years or older undergoing PICC insertion, with the PICC expected to remain for at least 14 days, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 2 or less were randomly assigned (1:1:1) using a permuted block design and stratified by site and diagnosis of active cancer to receive a single intravenous infusion of amrecibart (300 mg; anti-FXI A2 domain monoclonal antibody), cenvacibart (250 mg; anti-FXI catalytic domain monoclonal antibody), or placebo. Participants, principal investigators, and study site staff were masked to treatment assignment. The primary efficacy outcome was adjudicated venous thromboembolism (symptomatic or asymptomatic PICC-associated deep vein thrombosis or superficial vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism, including pulmonary embolism-related death) up to day 14. Ultrasounds were performed on days 7 and 14. The key secondary efficacy outcome was adjudicated thrombosis detected by ultrasound in the upper extremity with the PICC up to day 14. The primary safety outcome was site-reported treatment-emergent adverse events up to the end of the study. The key secondary safety outcomes were adjudicated major and clinically relevant non-major (CRNM) bleeding up to day 14. Efficacy analyses were performed in the full analysis set, which consisted of all randomly assigned participants who received any study drug and with any evaluable post-baseline ultrasound or a confirmed episode of venous thromboembolism. Safety analyses were performed in the safety analysis set, which included all randomly assigned participants who received any study drug (as treated). This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299111 (completed; these analyses were performed after database lock on May 6, 2026). FINDINGS: Between Sept 20, 2024, and Dec 19, 2025, 240 participants were screened, and 195 were randomly assigned to amrecibart (n=65), cenvacibart (n=66), or placebo (n=64). One participant in the placebo group who did not receive study treatment and had no evaluable ultrasound was excluded from the full analysis set. The median follow-up time was 100 days (IQR 100-103). The median age was 60 years (49-69), and 89 (46%) of 194 participants were female, 105 (54%) were male, and 192 (99%) were White. Adjudicated venous thromboembolism up to day 14 occured in 13 (20%) of 65 participants in the amrecibart group (odds ratio [OR] 0·37 [90% credible interval 0·18-0·65]), 13 (20%) of 66 participants in the cenvacibart group (0·36 [0·17-0·64]) compared with 27 (43%) of 63 participants in the placebo group. Adjudicated PICC-associated venous thromboembolism up to day 14 occurred in 12 (18%) participants in the amrecibart group (OR 0·30 [95% CI 0·14-0·67]), 13 (20%) participants in the cenvacibart group (0·32 [0·14-0·69]), compared with 27 (43%) participants in the placebo group. Site-reported treatment-emergent adverse events up to day 100 occurred in 45 (69%) participants in the amrecibart group, 42 (64%) participants in the cenvacibart group, and 48 (76%) participants in the placebo group. No participants had major bleeding up to day 14. CRNM bleeding up to day 14 occurred in two (3%) participants in the amrecibart group, two (3%) in the cenvacibart group, and two (3%) in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred in nine (14%) participants in the ambrecibart group, six (9%) in the cenvacibart group, and ten (16%) in the placebo group. One (2%) participant in the amrecibart group, four (6%) participants in the cenvacibart group, and two (3%) participants in the placebo group died; these deaths were assessed as not related to treatment by the respective investigators. INTERPRETATION: A single infusion of amrecibart or cenvacibart reduced the incidence of venous thromboembolism following PICC insertion, suggesting FXI inhibition at the A2 or catalytic domain as a promising prophylactic strategy for contact-mediated thrombosis. title: Endovascular treatment of hepatic artery bleeding and pseudoaneurysms using stent-grafts: a retrospective single-centre analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate technical and clinical success rates and complications of stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-centre retrospective study consecutively included 58 patients who underwent attempted stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding (n = 40) or pseudoaneurysm (n = 18) between January 2010 and June 2021. RESULTS: Technical success was achieved in 97% (56/58) of cases. Insufficient haemostasis after technical success was present in five cases (88% primary clinical success), decreasing to three cases after reintervention. In 3/5 cases, it was due to undersizing of the stent-graft, which occurred frequently, especially in vessel sizes ≥ 6 mm (n = 19, compared to the non-acute vessel diameter; n = 11, compared to the acute one). Median occlusion-free survival was 763 days. Patency rates were 81 ± 6% at 30 days and 56 ± 10% at two years. Early occlusion (≤ 30 days) was associated with significantly smaller stent-graft diameters (4.7 ± 0.7 mm vs 5.4 ± 0.7 mm; p = 0.014). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, a small diameter (4 mm) was confirmed as a risk factor for stent-graft occlusion (HR = 8.59, p = 0.006). Liver necrosis or liver failure due to insufficient collateralization occurred only in early occlusions. Median overall survival was 714 days. In 6/29 documented deaths, mortality was procedure-related (four because of insufficient haemostasis, with two after technical failure and two after technical success, and two because of fatal liver failure after stent-graft occlusion). CONCLUSION: Stent-grafting is effective for managing hepatic artery bleeding, but precise sizing is crucial, as undersizing and small diameters increase the risk of inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. KEY POINTS: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of stent-graft treatment for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm, and which factors influence these outcomes? Findings Stent-graft treatment achieved high technical and clinical success rates. Stent-graft undersizing and smaller stent-graft diameters were associated with inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. Clinical relevance Stent-graft treatment is an effective option for managing hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm in critically ill patients. Accurate stent-graft sizing is a key determinant of clinical success.

title: Saphenofemoral junction reconstruction and recurrence after the treatment of superficial venous reflux disease with endovenous ablation methods.
abstract: 2 p BackgroundRecurrence of varicosities and reflux-related symptoms after endovenous ablation of the great saphenous vein (GSV) remains common. Standard ablation is delivered 1.5-2 cm distal to the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ), leaving the junctional tributaries and dilated proximal junction untreated, unlike conventional high ligation and stripping. We compared standard endovenous ablation with a technique combining open SFJ reconstruction and endovenous ablation.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed patients treated for symptomatic primary GSV reflux. Group 1 underwent standard endovenous ablation (at our institution or referred from elsewhere). Group 2 underwent open SFJ reconstruction - ligation of the junctional tributaries, division of the saphenous vein, and reduction of the dilated common femoral vein - plus endovenous ablation of the GSV trunk. The protocol was introduced during the study period and applied selectively and non-randomly; patients with a body mass index ≥30 kg/m, those aged ≥70 years and those with groin skin infection received standard ablation. Beyond a 3-month review, duplex follow-up was not standardised and was performed mainly when symptoms recurred. Symptomatic recurrence, recurrent visible varicosities, duplex recurrence patterns, reintervention and complications were reported separately.ResultsGroup 1 included 115 patients (70 treated at our institution and 45 referred after treatment elsewhere) and Group 2 included 203. Mean age was 54.3 ± 10.9 and 48.7 ± 14.8 years, and 62.6% and 71.9% were female, respectively. Group 1 had a higher body mass index and more diabetes, hypertension and smoking (all P ≤ .003). During follow-up, 18 patients in Group 1 (15.7%) returned with symptomatic recurrence, compared with 7 (3.4%) in Group 2 (< .001; adjusted OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.05-0.40). No Group 2 patient showed a patent refluxing GSV trunk. In Group 2, six patients (3.0%) had groin wound complications, four managed with wound care and two requiring surgical revision, and one had a minor groin hematoma; one Group 1 patient developed deep vein thrombosis. There was no pulmonary embolism and no mortality.ConclusionsIn this selected, non-randomised cohort, adding open SFJ reconstruction to endovenous GSV ablation was associated with an acceptable complication rate, at the cost of reintroducing groin wound morbidity, and with lower symptomatic recurrence than standard ablation. Given the baseline imbalance, potential referral bias and non-standardised follow-up, these findings show an association rather than a preventive effect. Whether patients at particularly high risk of SFJ/anterior accessory saphenous vein-related recurrence benefit from this approach should be tested prospectively.

title: Perioperative venous thromboembolism prophylaxis during penile prosthesis surgery without routine drain placement: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Patients undergoing penile prosthesis surgery are at elevated risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet perioperative thromboprophylaxis is not addressed in current urologic guidelines and the safety of subcutaneous heparin (SqH) without drain placement remains unclear. We aim to evaluate the safety and efficacy of perioperative SqH for VTE prevention in penile prosthesis surgery performed without surgical drains. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all penile prosthesis surgeries performed at a single institution from January 2019 to January 2025 in which no drain was placed. Demographics, comorbidities, Caprini risk scores, VTE risk factors, hematoma incidence, and 90-day postoperative complications were compared between patients who did and did not receive perioperative SqH. RESULTS: The primary outcome of our study was postoperative VTE, with secondary outcomes including hematoma formation and 90-day complications. Of 524 patients, 85% were classified as high risk for VTE (Caprini ≥ 5). A total of 246 (47%) received perioperative SqH. VTE occurred in 0.7% (2/278) of patients who did not receive SqH, while no VTE was observed in the SqH group. Hematoma rates were similar between groups (SqH 2.0% vs non-SqH 2.2%; P = .920). Caprini scores and most comorbidities were comparable, though smoking (P = .043) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (P = .025) were more common in the non-SqH cohort. DISCUSSION: Implementation of VTE prophylaxis with SqH in penile prosthesis patients may reduce the risk of VTE in a high-risk population and is relatively cost effective and simple to implement. The main strength of this study is that it is the largest cohort of penile prosthesis patients receiving SqH to be analyzed. In addition, our patient population is unique in the lack of drain placement postoperatively. The study is limited by its retrospective nature and potential bias in reporting complications. The cohort of patients receiving SqH prophylaxis did not develop a VTE and adverse event rates were similar between groups suggesting a possible protective benefit without increasing postoperative complications.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all penile prosthesis surgeries performed at a single institution from January 2019 to January 2025 in which no drain was placed.

title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke: the BRETIS-TNK2 trial.
abstract: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during endovascular treatment (EVT) may increase first-pass recanalization and dissolve microcirculatory thrombi, but its efficacy and safety are uncertain. We hypothesised that this strategy would improve functional outcomes versus EVT alone. This phase 3, randomised, adaptive-enrichment, open-label, blinded-endpoint multicentre study aims to evaluate whether intra‑arterial tenecteplase improves clinical outcomes for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Patients with large‑vessel occlusion eligible for EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1) to the tenecteplase group receiving intra‑arterial tenecteplase during EVT or the control group receiving EVT alone. The primary endpoint was favorable functional outcome. Of 380 randomised patients (192 in the tenecteplase group and 188 in the control group), primary outcome data were available for 190 and 186 patients, respectively. Favorable 90-day functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) occurred in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 46.8% of the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 0.76, [95% CI 0.50-1.14], P = 0.19). This work suggests intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy did not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population. (Funded by National Science and Technology Major Project and hospital-initiated grants; ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT05657444).

title: Concurrent Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor and Factor Xa Inhibitor Use Is Associated With Increased Transfusion and Periprosthetic Joint Infection After Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty Despite Tranexamic Acid.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) impair platelet function, and concurrent SSRI and oral anticoagulant use has been associated with major bleeding in medical populations. We evaluated whether preoperative concurrent SSRI and factor Xa (FXa) inhibitor use was associated with higher transfusion and complication rates compared with use of either medication alone after primary total hip arthroplasty (THA) when tranexamic acid (TXA) use was standard. METHODS: Adult patients who underwent primary THA and received TXA on the day of surgery were identified in a large electronic health records database. The SSRI-only, FXa-only, and concurrent-use cohorts were independently 1:1 propensity-score matched to controls who did not have either exposure. The concurrent-use cohort was also matched directly to the SSRI-only and FXa-only cohorts. The primary outcome was allogeneic red blood cell transfusion. The secondary outcomes were surgical site infection (SSI), venous thromboembolism (VTE), periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), and revision THA at 30, 90, and 365 days. RESULTS: Compared with matched controls, SSRI-only patients had significantly higher transfusion, PJI, and revision THA rates at all timepoints (30-day transfusion risk ratio [RR] 1.44; 1-year PJI, RR 1.48; 1-year revision, RR 1.84; all P < 0.001). The FXa-only patients did not have higher transfusion or complication rates. Compared with SSRI-only patients, concurrent use was not associated with significantly different rates of any outcome at any timepoint. Compared with FXa-only use, concurrent use was associated with higher transfusion rates at all timepoints and higher PJI and revision rates at 90 days and one year (RR 1.54 to 2.12; all P ≤ 0.026). CONCLUSION: Preoperative SSRI use was associated with higher transfusion, PJI, and revision THA rates. Concurrent use exceeded FXa-only rates, but not SSRI-only rates, suggesting that SSRI use may be the more important perioperative risk marker. The use of SSRIs should be recognized during preoperative bleeding-risk assessment.

METHODS: Adult patients who underwent primary THA and received TXA on the day of surgery were identified in a large electronic health records database.

title: Prevalence of concomitant aneurysms in patients with thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms who underwent Fenestrated/Branched Endovascular Aortic Repair (F-BEVAR).
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the prevalence of synchronous ascending aortic and peripheral arterial aneurysms in patients with Crawford extent I-IV thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms (TAAA) undergoing fenestrated/branched endovascular aneurysm repair (F/BEVAR). METHODS: We performed a single-center retrospective review of prospectively collected data from patients with Crawford extent I-IV TAAA treated with F/BEVAR under a physician-sponsored investigational device exemption. The preoperative CTA obtained for device planning was used to measure the ascending aorta and bilateral common iliac (CIA), hypogastric (HA), and common femoral (CFA) arteries using centerline reconstruction. Bilateral popliteal artery (PA) diameters were obtained from preoperative arterial duplex imaging. An aneurysm was defined as a vessel diameter >50% greater than the expected normal diameter for that arterial bed, using references available from literature. Multivariable logistic regression included sex, obesity, race/ethnicity, TAAA diameter ≥7 cm, and prior aortic dissection. A sensitivity analysis was performed after excluding patients with prior aortic dissection. RESULTS: Among 249 patients (mean age, 70.8±8.6 years; 40.2% women), 177 (71.1%) had at least one concomitant aneurysm. Race/ethnicity was 75.1% NH-White, 21.7% NH-Black, 0.8% Hispanic, and 2.4% Other. Among evaluable patients, aneurysm prevalence was 12.0% in the ascending aorta (29/242), 62.8% in the CIA (140/223), 42.1% in the HA (98/233), 22.2% in the PA (51/230), and 9.6% in the CFA (22/228). On multivariable analysis, CIA aneurysm was associated with obesity, non-White race/ethnicity, and TAAA diameter ≥7 cm; HA aneurysm with male sex, obesity, and prior dissection; CFA aneurysm with male sex; PA aneurysm with male sex and prior dissection; and ascending aortic aneurysm with TAAA diameter ≥7 cm and prior dissection. After exclusion of 46 patients with prior dissection, concomitant aneurysms remained a common occurrence. CONCLUSIONS: Concomitant aneurysms are common in patients undergoing F/BEVAR for Crawford extent I-IV TAAA. Several associations remained significant after multivariable adjustment. These findings should be interpreted in the context of a single-center referral population, variable arterial-bed denominators, possible diffuse arteriomegaly, and residual confounding. The prevalence of PA aneurysm supports further evaluation of selective popliteal assessment; however, this study does not support a universal screening recommendation or establish an effect on management, outcomes, or cost.

title: Repair durability following fenestrated versus chimney endovascular repair for elective juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms: a multicenter cohort study.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare repair durability following elective fenestrated endovascular aneurysm repair (FEVAR) and chimney endovascular aneurysm repair (ChEVAR) for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms using complementary procedural, imaging, and clinical outcome measures. METHODS: 2 A retrospective multicenter cohort study was performed across five high-volume aortic referral centers. Consecutive patients undergoing elective FEVAR or ChEVAR for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms were included. Baseline characteristics, technical success, endoleaks, secondary aortic intervention, aneurysm sac remodeling, and target vessel patency were compared. Repair durability was assessed by integrating proximal seal integrity, longitudinal aneurysm sac remodeling, and freedom from secondary aortic intervention. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t test or the Mann-Whitney U test, and categorical variables using χor Fisher's exact tests. Statistical significance was defined as P < .05. RESULTS: A total of 130 patients underwent elective repair, including 77 treated with FEVAR and 53 with ChEVAR. Baseline demographic characteristics, aneurysm diameter, and duration of follow-up were similar between groups. Technical success was comparable (98.7% vs 98.1%; P = .76), and target vessel patency exceeded 95% in both cohorts (P = .38). Type Ia endoleak occurred less frequently following FEVAR than ChEVAR (1.3% vs 22.6%; P < .001), with a lower incidence of all Type I endoleaks (Types Ia, Ib, and Ic) (7.8% vs 26.4%; P = .006). Secondary aortic intervention was also less common following FEVAR (10.4% vs 30.2%; P = .006). Progressive aneurysm sac regression was observed following FEVAR, with a mean reduction of 11 mm at 24 months, whereas ChEVAR demonstrated limited early regression followed by late sac re-expansion, resulting in an overall 2-mm reduction. Mean aneurysm sac diameter was significantly smaller following FEVAR compared with ChEVAR at both 12 months (55 vs 59 mm; P = .01) and 24 months (51 vs 63 mm; P < .001). CONCLUSIONS: Elective FEVAR and ChEVAR achieved similarly high technical success and target vessel patency for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms. During mid-term follow-up, FEVAR was associated with lower rates of proximal attachment-site failure, greater aneurysm sac regression, and fewer secondary aortic interventions. These concordant procedural, imaging, and clinical outcomes suggest that integrated longitudinal assessment provides a more comprehensive evaluation of repair durability following complex endovascular aneurysm repair than technical success alone.

METHODS: 2 A retrospective multicenter cohort study was performed across five high-volume aortic referral centers. Consecutive patients undergoing elective FEVAR or ChEVAR for juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms were included.

title: Risk Prediction With a Type Ia-Oriented Proximal Neck Anatomic Severity Grading Score After EVAR.
abstract: BACKGROUND: We developed an exploratory Type Ia-oriented proximal neck Anatomic Severity Grading Score (Type Ia-ASGS) and assessed its association with postoperative type Ia endoleak after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). METHODS: We analyzed 304 elective standard EVAR patients treated during 2016-April 2024 with an Ankura endograft (Lifetech). Neck measurements were proximal diameter (A), distal diameter (B), and centerline length (C). The score assigned 1 point each for C ≤15 mm, max(A, B) >28 mm, and B - A ≥3 mm, and 2 points each for angulation >60° and calcification. The theoretical range was 0-7; weights reflected observed univariable associations. RESULTS: Mean clinical and imaging follow-up was 27.6 ± 3.2 months, with final follow-up in June 2026. Type Ia endoleak occurred in 14/304 patients (4.6%). Observed event proportions were 1.2%, 2.8%, and 28.1% in exploratory low (0-1), intermediate (2-3), and high (≥4) score categories (p < 0.001). Each point was associated with greater odds of type Ia endoleak (odds ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.80-4.29). Apparent area under the curve was 0.859 (bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 0.750-0.943). Individual event and censoring dates were unavailable for time-to-event analysis. CONCLUSIONS: The Type Ia-ASGS was associated with postoperative type Ia endoleak in this derivation cohort. Its heuristic weights and exploratory categories require independent validation before clinical use.

title: Temporal trend and geographic variation in anticoagulation of patients hospitalized with acute pulmonary embolism: the RIETE registry 2013-2024.
abstract: BACKGROUND: A recent U.S. study of initial anticoagulation in adults with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) requiring hospitalization found intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) use exceeded 50%. Guidelines, however, recommend low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) over UFH for most patients requiring parenteral anticoagulation. Use patterns in other geographic regions are unclear. METHODS: We analyzed data from RIETE, a prospective multinational registry of consecutive patients with venous thromboembolism. We included adults hospitalized for acute PE from 2013 through 2024 in 273 hospitals across 31 countries. We assessed temporal trend and regional variation in initial anticoagulation. Using multivariable regression, we identified variables independently associated with UFH. RESULTS: Among 36,210 adults, 83.2% received subcutaneous LMWH, 7.1% UFH, and 6.8% direct oral anticoagulants. LMWH use decreased slightly from 2013 to 2024 (85.8% to 79.2%; unadjusted), while UFH increased (8.9% to 10.4%). Wide geographic variation was observed in overall use of LMWH (37%--95%) and UFH (2%--39%). When adjusted for demographic and clinical covariates, increased weight, recent surgery, recent major bleeding, severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe renal dysfunction, abnormal vital signs, and early reperfusion therapy were positively associated, whereas age >80 years, active cancer, chronic lung disease, prior ischemic stroke, and year were negatively associated with UFH. Compared with Spanish hospitals, hospitals in other European countries, the United States, and Asia were independently associated with UFH use. CONCLUSIONS: Results highlight opportunities for some geographic regions to align anticoagulation practices more closely with evidence-based guidelines recommending LMWH as the preferred parenteral agent in most patients with PE requiring hospitalization.

title: Association between nasogastric tube placement and self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms in patients receiving endovascular thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion: A post-hoc analysis of the ENCHANTED2/MT trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-stroke anxiety and depression are common after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large vessel occlusion (LVO) and impair long-term recovery. Nasogastric tube (NGT) placement marks severe dysphagia and illness, but its association with anxiety or depression remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate whether NGT placement is associated with the presence and severity of 90-day self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms after successful EVT. METHODS: We performed a post-hoc analysis of the ENCHANTED2/MT multicentre randomized controlled trial, including patients with anterior-circulation LVO who achieved successful reperfusion and had complete 90-day EQ-5D-3 L data. Participants were stratified by in-hospital NGT placement (No-NGT group vs. NGT group). The primary outcome was self-reported anxiety/depression assessed by the EQ-5D-3 L dimension (no, moderate, or extreme symptoms). We explored the association between NGT placement and the proportion and severity of self-reported anxiety/depression using propensity score matching (PSM) and logistic regression, and performed exploratory subgroup analyses. RESULTS: Of 575 patients, 280(48.7%) received an NGT. Before matching, the proportion reporting self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms was 38.6% in the NGT group versus 15.6% in the no-NGT group (unadjusted OR3.40, 95%CI 2.30-5.09). After adjustment for measured clinical covariates, the association remained significant (adjusted OR2.97, 95%CI 1.93-4.63; ordinal OR3.06, 95%CI 1.99-4.77). After PSM, 175 patients were matched in each group; NGT placement remained associated with higher odds of self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms (37.7% vs 21.1%; OR2.26, 95%CI 1.41-3.65; ordinal OR2.25, 95%CI 1.41-3.63). In exploratory subgroup analyses, the association appeared more pronounced in patients with admission NIHSS ≤ 15 (OR3.83, 95% CI1.82-8.07; P for interaction = 0.049). CONCLUSION: In this post-hoc analysis, NGT placement was associated with higher odds of self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms.NGT requirement may identify patients who deserve closer psychological assessment.

Nasogastric tube (NGT) placement marks severe dysphagia and illness, but its association with anxiety or depression remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate whether NGT placement is associated with the presence and severity of 90-day self-reported anxiety/depression symptoms after successful EVT.

title: Predictors of longer recognition time in acute aortic dissection: a retrospective observational study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) carries a high mortality risk closely tied to diagnostic timeliness. Delays remain prevalent, driven by atypical presentations-particularly in patients without a chief complaint of pain. This study identified predictors of a longer recognition time, as indicated by prolonged door-to-CT times, and developed a cumulative prediction model for patients presenting without pain complaints. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of 197 adult patients diagnosed with AAD at a tertiary emergency department (ED) from 2016 to 2023. Patients were classified as having a shorter (< 74 min) or longer (≥ 74 min; cohort median) door-to-CT completion time. Predictors were identified by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-penalized logistic regression and decision tree analysis. A subgroup analysis characterized pain-complaint-free patients using a stepwise identification algorithm. RESULTS: A longer door-to-CT time was associated with female sex, older age, and physiological instability. The strongest multivariable predictors were absence of abrupt pain (odds ratio [OR] 2.81, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.47-5.46) and non-severe triage classification (OR 4.70, 95% CI 1.71-15.29). Dyspnea (OR 2.14) and elevated diastolic blood pressure (OR 1.02/mmHg) also independently predicted a longer door-to-CT time. Among pain-complaint-free patients (n = 46), a stepwise combination of mediastinal widening on chest radiography, Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥ 3, and Shock Index > 1.0 was present in all identified cases (cumulative case coverage 46/46; 95% CI 92.3%-100%). CONCLUSION: This study identifies a high-risk profile for a longer recognition time of AAD, particularly in older female patients and those presenting without sudden pain. For patients unable to report pain, chest radiography, shock index, and comorbidity burden may be considered to help identify atypical presentations warranting urgent evaluation.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) carries a high mortality risk closely tied to diagnostic timeliness. Delays remain prevalent, driven by atypical presentations-particularly in patients without a chief complaint of pain. This study identified predictors of a longer recognition time, as indicated by prolonged door-to-CT times, and developed a cumulative prediction model for patients presenting without pain complaints.

title: Real-world safety of intrasaccular flow disruption for unruptured cerebral aneurysms: a multicenter analysis of on-label versus off-label aneurysm location treatment in the NeuroVascular Quality Initiative-Quality Outcomes Database registry.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Intrasaccular flow disruption (IFD) has been shown to be safe and efficacious in the treatment of unruptured cerebral aneurysms. However, previous studies were typically performed at large-volume centers, were carefully curated, and devices were used in on-label locations. The purpose of this study was to examine IFD safety using real-world data, in both on-label and off-label aneurysm locations. METHODS: The NeuroVascular Quality Initiative-Quality Outcomes Database registry was analyzed for all unruptured aneurysms treated with IFD. On-label versus off-label treatment locations were compared. The primary outcome was the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score at discharge. Secondary outcomes included intraoperative complications, mRS score at last follow-up, and aneurysm occlusion status. Direct comparisons between groups were performed first, and results were confirmed with propensity score matching. RESULTS: There were 329 (82%) on-label aneurysm location treatments and 72 (18%) off-label treatments. The mean patient age was 64.6 years (range 27-86 years). On-label aneurysms were slightly larger than off-label aneurysms, with a mean maximum dimension of 6.9 mm versus 6.2 mm (p = 0.041). Otherwise, there were no significant differences in group characteristics. The mean follow-up was 512 days. There was no significant difference for the primary outcome of mRS score at discharge (mRS score ≤ 2: 94.1% on-label vs 97.5% off-label, p = 0.615). There were no significant differences for secondary outcomes including any intraoperative complication (3.6% vs 2.8%, p > 0.999), mRS score at last follow-up, and aneurysm occlusion status at discharge (Raymond-Roy class 1: 54.1% vs 56%, p = 0.929). There were significant missing data for occlusion status at the last follow-up, precluding analysis. Propensity score matching yielded 68 patients in each group and confirmed no significant differences for primary and secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: This largest-to-date prospective registry study supports the overall safety of IFD treatment for unruptured cerebral aneurysms in both on-label and off-label aneurysm locations. Questions remain regarding long-term efficacy due to current follow-up data limitations in the registry.

The purpose of this study was to examine IFD safety using real-world data, in both on-label and off-label aneurysm locations.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models in Vascular Surgery Cases: Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are increasingly used by clinicians, yet their accuracy, safety, and consistency in clinical cases remain poorly defined. Most studies assess LLMs using multiple-choice questions rather than free-response reasoning. OBJECTIVE: The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the performance and safety of 3 widely used LLMs in realistic vascular surgery scenarios in key domains such as diagnosis, investigation, and multidisciplinary and multimodal management. The secondary objective of this study was to evaluate the safety of the models' outputs. METHODS: t A total of 42 fictitious vascular cases across 5 major pathologies (acute limb ischemia [ALI], aortopathy, chronic limb ischemia, diabetic foot infection, and extracranial cerebrovascular disease) were independently entered into GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 using standardized prompts. Each model answered structured questions covering diagnosis, investigation, and management (both operative and nonoperative). Responses were scored out of 20 by a panel using a predefined rubric. Each plan's overall safety was separately assessed. Comparative analyses used 2-tailedtests, ANOVA, and multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: P P P P Mean composite scores by model were 86.5% for ChatGPT, 83.5% for Gemini, and 88.0% for Claude, whereas scores by disease were 82.7% for ALI, 83.8% for aortopathy, 85.9% for chronic limb ischemia, 86.1% for diabetic foot infection, and 80.7% for extracranial cerebrovascular disease (>.05 in each case). Unsafe plans were generated in 11.9%, 23.8%, and 7.1% of cases by ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, respectively. On multivariable analysis, independent predictors of unsafe outputs were lower composite score (odds ratio [OR] 0.471, 95% CI 0.306-0.722;=.001), higher word count (OR 1.003, 95% CI 1.001-1.005;=.001), and ALI (OR 20.9, 95% CI 3.79-61.8;<.001). CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate LLMs' promise in managing routine vascular surgery cases. However, their inconsistent safety profiles and ethical limitations preclude unsupervised clinical use. Rigorous specialty-specific validation is essential before they may be integrated into routine practice.

title: Effects of angiotensin receptor blockers on aortic growth and clinical events in Marfan syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is a major cause of aortic dissection and premature mortality in Marfan syndrome. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) may slow aortic enlargement, but their effects on clinical and imaging outcomes remain uncertain. The aim of the study is to evaluate the effects of ARBs on clinical events and aortic growth in patients with Marfan syndrome. We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, and Web of Science through February 1, 2025. Acute aortic dissection and all-cause mortality were the primary outcomes. Binary outcomes were analyzed using both Mantel-Haenszel common-effect (MH-CE) and inverse-variance random-effects (IV-RE) models. For outcomes with an event incidence below 10% in every contributing study, the MH-CE estimate was emphasized and the IV-RE estimate was treated as a sensitivity analysis. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using IV-RE models. All analyses were conducted with the meta package in R (v4.3.2). Seven randomized controlled trials involving 1522 patients with Marfan syndrome were included in the main analysis. For acute aortic dissection, the MH-CE estimate was RR 0·62 (95% CI 0·24-1·59) and the IV-RE estimate was RR 0·62 (95% CI 0·20-1·92). For all-cause mortality, the corresponding estimates were RR 0·53 (95% CI 0·17-1·64) and RR 0·58 (95% CI 0·16-2·07). Confidence intervals were wide and crossed unity. ARBs were associated with less aortic-root growth measured by MRI (MD - 0·48 mm/year, 95% CI - 0·89 to - 0·08) and by echocardiography over 3 years (MD - 0·51 mm/3 years, 95% CI - 0·85 to - 0·17), whereas annual echocardiographic measurement showed no significant difference (MD - 0·06 mm/year, 95% CI - 0·22 to 0·10). No significant effect was observed on ascending-aortic diameter, aortic Z-score at 3 years, aortic surgery, or serious adverse events. No statistically significant effect modification was detected in exploratory subgroup analyses. In patients with Marfan syndrome, ARB therapy was associated with small reductions in aortic-root growth in selected imaging analyses but did not significantly reduce acute aortic dissection or all-cause mortality. Sparse events, wide confidence intervals, and limited follow-up preclude firm conclusions regarding clinical benefit. Adequately powered, long-term trials with standardized imaging and clinical outcomes are required.
englishSummary: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is a major cause of aortic dissection and premature mortality in Marfan syndrome. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) may slow aortic enlargement, but their effects on clinical and imaging outcomes remain uncertain. The aim of the study is to evaluate the effects of ARBs on clinical events and aortic growth in patients with Marfan syndrome.

title: Personalized anticoagulation and drug monitoring for pregnancy-associated venous thromboembolism in hereditary type IIa antithrombin deficiency.
abstract: Pregnant women with hereditary type IIa antithrombin deficiency (ATD) are at significantly increased thrombotic risk. We present the case of a woman with four consecutive pregnancy losses due to venous thromboembolism (VTE), subsequently diagnosed with type IIa hereditary ATD. Type IIa ATD is exceptionally rare. The principal therapeutic challenge lies in the absence of established guidelines regarding optimal anticoagulant selection, dosing strategies, and monitoring approaches for such patients, contributing to treatment failure in her first four pregnancies. The patient was referred to our institution before her fifth conception. Preconception intervention began, and we instituted low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) therapy, with dose titration guided by thrombin-antithrombin complex (TAT) and anti-Xa activity levels. This regimen demonstrated safety and efficacy, achieving a maximum nadroparin dose of 10 250 IU twice daily. Under close pharmacotherapeutic monitoring by a clinical pharmacist using this individualized protocol, the patient achieved a successful term delivery and was discharged.

title: Perioperative combined intravenous and intra-articular tranexamic acid does not increase venous thromboembolism risk after total knee arthroplasty in plateau areas: a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: After total knee arthroplasty (TKA), rivaroxaban is often used to prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE), while tranexamic acid (TXA) is used to reduce perioperative bleeding. However, plateau hypoxia may affect coagulation. We assessed whether combined intravenous and intra-articular TXA increases VTE risk in plateau TKA patients. This single-center, prospective, randomized, double-blind, pilot controlled trial was conducted at altitude greater than 3500 m. Fifty unilateral TKA patients were randomized to experimental (intravenous + intra-articular TXA) or control (intravenous TXA alone). All received rivaroxaban for 14 days. Primary outcome was new-onset DVT (deep vein thrombosis) or PE (Pulmonary Embolism) at day 3; secondary outcomes included thromboelastography (TEG) and coagulation parameters at 6 h, 1, 2, and 3 days. No VTE occurred in either group. Nonthrombotic ultrasound findings (intermuscular vein dilation with blood stasis) were observed in 9/25 (36%) of the experimental group and 13/25 (52%) of the control group, with no between-group difference (P = 0.254). TEG parameters showed no significant differences, except for a transiently lower D-dimer in the experimental group on day 1 (P < 0.001), though clinical relevance is unclear. Hb and Hct declined less in the experimental group at all time points (P < 0.05), suggesting reduced blood loss. In plateau TKA patients, adding intra-articular TXA to intravenous TXA did not increase short-term VTE risk. These preliminary findings suggest combined TXA with rivaroxaban may be well tolerated in this population.

title: The effect of renal denervation on blood pressure in patients with chronic kidney disease (RDN-CKD Study): Results of a multicentre, prospective, randomized, sham-controlled and blinded investigator-initiated trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Endovascular ultrasound renal denervation (uRDN) offers the opportunity to modulate sympathetic nervous system activity, thereby lowering blood pressure (BP) and potentially improving or stabilizing renal outcomes. OBJECTIVE: We hypothesized that in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 and uncontrolled hypertension, endovascular ultrasound-based RDN will lower BP after 6 months. METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, randomized, sham-controlled, blinded, clinical trial, investigated the effects of uRDN or sham in patients with CKD stage 3 and uncontrolled hypertension. The primary and secondary endpoints were changes in ambulatory BP (ABP) and office BP at 6 months. The study was prematurely stopped due to slow enrollment. RESULTS: Twenty subjects (uRDN: N  = 10, sham: N  = 10) completed the 6-month visit. At 6 months, the sham-corrected change from baseline in 24 h systolic ABP was -5.60 mmHg (95% CI -10.7, -0.54 mmHg; P  = 0.170). The sham corrected change from baseline in 24-h diastolic ABP was -5.90 mmHg (95% CI -9.25, -2.55; P  = 0.035) and from baseline daytime ABP -6.85 mmHg (95% CI -10.6, -3.08; P  = 0.030). Sensitivity analysis restricting the analysis to those patients who were fully adherent to medication ( N  = 7 in each group) found a sham-corrected change from baseline 24-h diastolic ABP of -5.71 mmHg (95% CI -9.40, -2.03; P  = 0.053) at 6 months. Based on the composite endpoint of 24 h ABP and office BP for systolic/diastolic BP, a win ratio of 1.71 (95% 1.26-2.34; P  = 0.014) was found for systolic BP and a win ratio of 4.59 (95% CI 2.94-7.16, P  < 0.001) was found for diastolic BP, indicating significant changes in BP following RDN. Estimated glomerular filtration rate remained stable over 6 months, with no difference between the groups. There were no safety signals associated with uRDN. CONCLUSIONS: This prospective randomized, sham controlled, blinded trial in patients with uncontrolled hypertension and CKD was prematurely stopped, resulted in small number of patients and we did not find a statistically significant effect on systolic BP, whereas a consistent reduction in diastolic BP following uRDN was observed. These data should guide the design of a larger confirmatory trial in patients with CKD.

OBJECTIVE: We hypothesized that in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3 and uncontrolled hypertension, endovascular ultrasound-based RDN will lower BP after 6 months. METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, randomized, sham-controlled, blinded, clinical trial, investigated the effects of uRDN or sham in patients with CKD stage 3 and uncontrolled hypertension.

title: Discontinuation of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors before non-cardiac surgery: a meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The best management approach for renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitor use before surgery is controversial. Some studies have suggested that continuation could increase the risk of clinically significant peri-operative hypotension and, thus, organ injury. By contrast, others believe that withholding them significantly increases the risk of severe hypertension and heart failure. To determine the most effective strategy, this systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials compared discontinuation vs continuation of RAS inhibitors in patients undergoing non-cardiac and non-vascular surgeries. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) databases were searched for randomized controlled trials that compared discontinuation vs continuation of RAS inhibitors in patients undergoing non-cardiac and non-vascular surgery. RESULTS: Five randomized controlled trials (n = 10 773 patients; 5388 randomized to discontinuation) were included. Discontinuation of an RAS inhibitor probaby reduced peri-operative hypotension (27.66% vs 34.06%; risk ratio [RR] 0.81, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73-0.89; moderate certainty). The evidence is very uncertain about effects on peri-operative hypertension (9.46% vs 8.05%; RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.66-2.89; very low certainty). For major clinical outcomes, discontinuation suggested little to no difference in acute kidney injury (10.45% vs 10.69%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.66-1.45; low certainty), acute heart failure (5.38% vs 5.32%; RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.76-1.31; low certainty), myocardial infarction (1.22% vs 1.00%; RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.60-2.39; low certainty), stroke (0.42% vs 0.40%; RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.56-1.93; low certainty), and arrhythmias (1.80% vs 1.40%; RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.69-2.38; low certainty). CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that discontinuation of RAS inhibitors is likely to reduce peri-operative hypotension in patients undergoing non-cardiac, non-vascular surgery, but the evidence is very uncertain about effects on peri-operative hypertension and major clinical outcomes.

title: Efficacy of tranexamic acid in reducing perioperative blood loss and transfusion requirements following limb-salvage surgery for bone tumors: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract: BackgroundLimb salvage surgery with endoprosthetic reconstruction for malignant bone tumors is frequently associated with substantial perioperative blood loss and high transfusion requirements. Although tranexamic acid (TXA) has demonstrated efficacy in reducing blood loss in total joint arthroplasty, high-level evidence supporting its use in orthopaedic oncology remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial between April 2023 and September 2025. Thirty-six patients undergoing tumor resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction of the femur(Proximal/distal/total), proximal tibia, or proximal humerus were randomized to receive either intravenous TXA (15 mg/kg at induction; n = 18) or placebo (n = 18). The primary outcome was calculated total blood loss at 72 hours using the hemoglobin balance method. Secondary outcomes included transfusion requirements, postoperative hemoglobin concentration, drain output, hospital stay, wound complications, and thromboembolic events. All patients completed a minimum follow-up of six weeks.ResultsMean calculated blood loss at 72 hours was lower in the TXA group than in the control group (995 ± 324 mL versus 1708 ± 508 mL; mean difference 713 mL; p < 0.001). Patients receiving TXA required fewer packed red blood cell transfusions (1.1 ± 0.7 versus 1.7 ± 0.7 units; mean difference 0.6 units; p = 0.01). Postoperative hemoglobin concentration was higher in the TXA group (9.3 ± 1.1 versus 8.7 ± 0.9 g/dL), although this difference was not significant (p = 0.073). No differences were observed in drain output, wound complications, or hospital stay. No symptomatic deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism occurred in either group.ConclusionIn this single-center randomized controlled trial, tranexamic acid was associated with reduced calculated total blood loss at 72 hours. However, the relatively small sample size limits conclusions regarding uncommon adverse events. Larger multicenter randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings and further evaluate safety across diverse orthopaedic oncology settings.

title: Hybrid Occipital Artery-AICA Bypass Followed by Endovascular Embolization for a Radiation-Induced Dissecting AICA Aneurysm in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND IMPORTANCE: Pediatric anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) aneurysms are rare; radiation-associated dissecting lesions require exclusion without compromising brainstem or cerebellar perforators. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: A 13-year-old boy developed a progressively enlarging right AICA a2 dissecting aneurysm after cranial irradiation for pineal nongerminomatous germ cell tumor. Because direct clipping or isolated parent vessel occlusion was considered high risk, he underwent occipital artery-AICA a3 bypass followed by endovascular coil embolization in a single hybrid session. Dual arterial access enabled transradial vertebral artery treatment and transfemoral angiographic bypass assessment. Postoperative MRI showed a small transient cerebellar ischemic lesion that resolved within 2 weeks. At 2 months, the patient was neurologically intact with patent bypass and no aneurysm recurrence. CONCLUSION: Hybrid occipital artery-AICA bypass followed by endovascular embolization is a feasible flow-preserving option for selected pediatric AICA aneurysms requiring distal perfusion preservation.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Rivaroxaban versus LMWH Thromboprophylaxis Following Gynecologic Cancer Surgery: A Retrospective Comparison Study.
abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to evaluate the clinical outcomes of rivaroxaban vs low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for thromboprophylaxis following gynecologic cancer surgery. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective comparative study of rivaroxaban vs standard LMWH in patients undergoing gynecologic malignancy surgery. Clinical outcomes included venous thromboembolism (VTE), major bleeding, non-major bleeding, and 1-year all-cause mortality. A multivariable logistic regression model was used to adjust for potential confounding factors. RESULTS: A total of 250 women were included, 134 received rivaroxaban and 116 received LMWH for postoperative thromboprophylaxis following gynecologic malignancy-related surgery. After adjusting for potential confounding factors using multivariable logistic regression, the 30-day VTE and bleeding events showed no significant differences between the rivaroxaban group and the LMWH groups. There were no cases of 30-day readmission related to surgery, no 30-day mortality, and no all-cause mortality during the 1-year follow-up. Notably, all distal DVT events in both groups were calf muscular vein thromboses. During the 1-year follow-up, no patients were rehospitalized or died due to VTE. CONCLUSION: We observed no significant differences in short- and long-term outcomes between rivaroxaban and LMWH after gynecologic malignancy surgery. Given the retrospective design and limited number of events, these results should be interpreted with caution, and prospective randomized studies are warranted.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective comparative study of rivaroxaban vs standard LMWH in patients undergoing gynecologic malignancy surgery. Clinical outcomes included venous thromboembolism (VTE), major bleeding, non-major bleeding, and 1-year all-cause mortality.

title: Development and Temporal Validation of a Thromboelastography-Based Nomogram for Queensland-Defined High Thrombotic Risk in Postpartum Women.
abstract: This study developed and temporally validated a nomogram that integrates thromboelastography (TEG) and maternal clinical factors to identify women classified as having high thrombotic risk according to the 2020 Queensland Clinical Guideline at postpartum reassessment after 24 h. The derivation cohort included 447 women who delivered at Foshan Women and Children Hospital between January 1, 2021, and December 27, 2022; 346 had Queensland scores of 0-2 and 101 had scores of ≥3. A same-center temporal validation cohort included 207 women who delivered between December 28, 2022, and February 14, 2025. Candidate clinical and TEG variables were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression, and model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration, and decision curve analysis. The final model retained hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, maternal age, current body mass index, native-cup TEG reaction time (R), and 24-h postpartum blood loss. Discrimination was acceptable in the derivation cohort (area under the curve [AUC], 0.791; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.737-0.845; sensitivity, 70.3%; specificity, 77.2%) and good in the temporal validation cohort (AUC, 0.847; 95% CI, 0.771-0.923; sensitivity, 75.8%; specificity, 85.6%). The model estimates Queensland-defined high thrombotic risk rather than objectively confirmed venous thromboembolism. It may support simplified postpartum reassessment after the first 24 h, but multicenter validation against objectively confirmed thrombotic outcomes is required before claims regarding event prediction or clinical implementation can be made.

title: In Vitro Passive Sealing Stent-Grafts for Chimney Endovascular Repair:Examination and a Japanese Single-Centre Retrospective Study.
abstract: PURPOSE: Juxtarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms (JAAAs) present with a short infrarenal neck that does not permit standard endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). The AFX VELA cuff extension with its endoskeletal architecture may reduce type Ia endoleak (TIaEL) through passive sealing. We examined this hypothesis using a double-chimney benchtop model and a clinical cohort treated with VELA-based chimney EVAR (ChEVAR). MATERIALS AND METHODS: A benchtop model compared gutter leakage volumes among VELA, Endurant II and Excluder C3 (5 trials per device). A retrospective single-centre cohort (January 2018-April 2024) included consecutive JAAA patients undergoing VELA-based ChEVAR with ≥12-month follow-up. Postoperative computed tomographic (CT) morphometry compared seal-zone geometry across the 3 platforms. RESULTS: In the benchtop model, VELA showed a median gutter leakage of 5.0 mL/min (interquartile range [IQR], 4.0-11.0), whereas both comparators exceeded 500 mL/min and were right-censored. In the clinical cohort, 20 patients (55% male; median age 80.0 years) underwent ChEVAR for JAAAs with a median diameter of 53.5 mm and infrarenal neck length of 5.0 mm. Clinically successful sac exclusion was achieved in 19 of 20 patients (95%). Intraoperative TIaEL occurred in 5 patients: 1 major endoleak was sealed with adjunctive gutter coil embolisation, and 4 minor endoleaks resolved spontaneously on the 1-month CT angiogram. Over a median follow-up of 36.5 months, no persistent TIaEL was detected on follow-up imaging, and no chimney stent-graft (SG) occlusion occurred. One patient (5%) required an aortic-related reintervention for a type Ib endoleak. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decreased by ≥20% in 9 patients (45%), and 1 started dialysis at 4 years. On postoperative CT morphometry, relative gutter area was lowest with VELA, intermediate with Endurant II and highest with Excluder C3; circumferential apposition followed the inverse pattern. CONCLUSION: In the benchtop model, VELA produced consistently lower leakage than both comparators, with concordant CT morphometric evidence consistent with a passive sealing mechanism. In this cohort, VELA-based ChEVAR achieved clinically successful sac exclusion in 19 of 20 patients (95%) with no persistent TIaEL and no chimney SG occlusion. These findings support the feasibility of VELA-based ChEVAR when FEVAR is unavailable; multicentre prospective validation is required. CLINICAL IMPACT: Persistent type Ia endoleak (TIaEL) is a principal limitation of chimney EVAR (ChEVAR) compared with fenestrated EVAR (FEVAR). We report short-to mid-term outcomes of ChEVAR using the AFX VELA cuff extension, whose endoskeletal architecture is designed to promote passive sealing. Postoperative CT morphometry comparing the 3 devices (VELA, Endurant II and Excluder C3) showed a smaller relative gutter area and higher circumferential apposition with VELA, paralleling the benchtop pattern. VELA-based ChEVAR achieved clinically successful sac exclusion in 19 of 20 patients (95%), without persistent TIaEL detected on follow-up imaging. VELA-based ChEVAR appears feasible when FEVAR is unavailable; however, multicentre validation is required.

We examined this hypothesis using a double-chimney benchtop model and a clinical cohort treated with VELA-based chimney EVAR (ChEVAR).

title: Pharmacogenomics guided clopidogrel utilization in veterans undergoing peripheral arterial intervention with vascular surgery compared to usual care.
abstract: After revascularization, patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) are at risk for ischemia. CYP2C19 variants may impact outcomes in those receiving clopidogrel but data is limited in PAD. This pilot study evaluated pharmacogenomic (PGx) guided care in 146 adult patients who underwent revascularization and were prescribed P2Y12 inhibitors. PGx testing was compared to no testing, with 61 patients in the PGx group vs 85 in control (clopidogrel only group). Clopidogrel was used in 97% of patients at baseline. Use of aspirin (64.7% vs 85.2%; p < 0.01) as well as stent interventions (44.7% vs 80%; p < 0.01) were less frequent in the control group, but P2Y12 inhibitor therapy duration was longer (10.2 ± 3.4 vs 8.0 ± 4.0 months; p < 0.04). Roughly one-third of patients were switched from clopidogrel based on PGx. Overall, in the control group, the composite of major adverse limb and cardiovascular events (45.9% vs 32.8%; p = 0.11), as well as bleeding events (14.1% vs 9.8%; p = 0.43) were non-significantly higher. At 7-12 months after revascularization, ischemic events were significantly lower in the PGx group (21.3% vs 4.7%; p = 0.01). A majority of ischemic events in the PGx group occurred within 90 days, and timely PGx testing was found to be delayed.
englishSummary: After revascularization, patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) are at risk for ischemia. CYP2C19 variants may impact outcomes in those receiving clopidogrel but data is limited in PAD. This pilot study evaluated pharmacogenomic (PGx) guided care in 146 adult patients who underwent revascularization and were prescribed P2Y12 inhibitors.

title: Comparative outcomes of endovascular versus synthetic bypass for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions: A 3-year single-center cohort study.
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) ranges from intermittent claudication to critical limb‑threatening ischemia (CLTI), with <3% of intermittent claudication cases progressing to CLTI. This study aimed to compare the outcomes of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting (PTAS) and synthetic graft femoropopliteal bypass (FPB) in a homogeneous PAD cohort. A subgroup analysis of TransAtlantic Inter-Society Consensus (TASC) B and C lesions, which lack standardized treatment algorithms, was also performed. We retrospectively analyzed 88 patients with no prior history of vascular interventions in the same limb who were treated for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions between 2016 and 2020 (29 underwent PTAS and 59 underwent FPB). Primary outcomes were reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, and vessel patency (primary, assisted primary, and secondary) over a 3‑year follow‑up. Subgroup analysis was performed to assess differences in treatment outcomes. No statistically significant differences were detected in reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, or patency between the two treatments. For loss of primary patency, the hazard ratio (HR) for FPB versus PTAS was 1.89 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.76-4.69; log-rank p = 0.146) and 1.23 (95% CI, 0.45-3.38) after adjustment for lesion length and TASC grade. In the TASC B and C subgroup, no significant differences were observed in primary, assisted primary, or secondary patency (log-rank p = 0.809, 0.302, and 0.135, respectively). The study was underpowered to detect modest effects (post-hoc power for primary patency, 34.4%). In this small single-center cohort, no statistically significant difference in 3-year outcomes was detected between PTAS and FPB for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions; clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded, and the findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.

This study aimed to compare the outcomes of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting (PTAS) and synthetic graft femoropopliteal bypass (FPB) in a homogeneous PAD cohort. A subgroup analysis of TransAtlantic Inter-Society Consensus (TASC) B and C lesions, which lack standardized treatment algorithms, was also performed.

title: Aspirin is safe and effective for prevention of deep vein thrombosis following acetabular fracture surgery.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with acetabular fractures are at significant risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet the optimal chemoprophylactic agent remains undefined. Emerging evidence from elective arthroplasty and general orthopaedic trauma populations suggests that aspirin (ASA) may be a safe and effective alternative to traditional anticoagulants. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ASA compared to other anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention following acetabular fracture surgery. METHODS: A retrospective cohort analysis was performed using a global, web-based health research network that provides on-demand access to de-identified, real-world data from electronic health records and claims. Adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent surgical treatment for acetabular fractures between January 2014 and December 2025 and received VTE prophylaxis within 14 days of surgery were identified. Patients were stratified into ASA (n = 1189) and other anticoagulant (n = 5478) cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to balance baseline characteristics, yielding 1174 patients per cohort. Rates and odds of DVT, emergency department (ED) visits, deep infection, stroke, and readmission were assessed at 14-, 30-, and 90-day postoperative intervals. Temporal trends in VTE prophylaxis utilization were also analyzed. RESULTS: Compared to other anticoagulants, ASA was associated with significantly lower odds of DVT at 14 days (1.11% vs. 2.22%; odds ratio [OR]: 0.494; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.253-0.967; P = 0.036), 30 days (1.45% vs. 2.73%; OR: 0.524; 95% CI: 0.290-0.950; P = 0.030), and 90 days (2.56% vs. 4.34%; OR: 0.577; 95% CI: 0.365-0.913; P = 0.018). ASA was also associated with significantly lower odds of ED visits at 90 days (OR: 0.741; 95% CI: 0.570-0.963; P = 0.024). There were no significant differences in deep infection, stroke, or readmission rates. ASA utilization increased from 7.2% in 2014-39.5% in 2025. CONCLUSIONS: ASA is safe and effective for DVT prevention following acetabular fracture surgery and is associated with fewer ED visits compared to other anticoagulants. These findings support the growing adoption of ASA as a VTE prophylactic agent in the acetabular fracture population.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Patients with acetabular fractures are at significant risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet the optimal chemoprophylactic agent remains undefined. Emerging evidence from elective arthroplasty and general orthopaedic trauma populations suggests that aspirin (ASA) may be a safe and effective alternative to traditional anticoagulants. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ASA compared to other anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention following acetabular fracture surgery.

title: Prediction models for venous thromboembolism in pediatric patients: A protocol for systematic review and critical appraisal.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) in children is a severe disease with high mortality rates. It is also gradually recognized as a major source of morbidity in hospitalized children, leading to increased length of hospital stay, higher mortality, and increased costs. The majority of pediatric subjects with VTE present inherited or acquired risk factors,such as the use of a central venous catheter (CVC), which accounts for more than more than 90% of neonatal VTE and 50% of pediatric VTE. Clinical studies on predictive models for VTE in children have shown inconsistent results. This systematic review aims to evaluate published prediction models for pediatric VTE, analyzing their characteristics, predictors, efficacy, and the methodological quality and applicability. The protocol has been prepared using the Preferred Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines. The systematic review protocol for VTE prediction in pediatric patients has been registered on PROSPERO (PROSPERO 2025CRD420251231316. Available from https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/vi-ew/CRD420251231316.) A comprehensive search across five major databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang) will be conducted for studies on prediction models of VTE among pediatric patients. Two researchers will independently screen literature, extract data, and evaluate the bias risk and applicability of included studies using prediction modelling study tools. This systematic review will provide critical insights into the efficacy and quality of reporting of the VTE model in pediatric patients. This will guide clinical physicians in selecting the most appropriate VTE prediction model and inform future research endeavors in pediatric VTE prediction.

title: SEQuential tUnneled Catheters and Infective Events in haemodiaLysis: A Five-Year Retrospective Cohort Study (SEQUEL Study).
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tunnelled-cuffed catheters (TCCs) are widely used for haemodialysis access when permanent vascular access is unavailable. Internal jugular vein (IJV) placement is guideline-preferred, but femoral vein (FV) catheters are frequently used when upper venous access is limited. Whether femoral access confers a higher infection risk than catheter sequence number remains unclear. This study evaluated these two competing determinants of catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI). METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included all TCC insertions at a tertiary nephrology unit between January 2016 and December 2021. The primary analysis examined CRBSI incidence per 1000 catheter-days stratified by catheter sequence number (first, second, third+ insertion per patient). Secondary analyses compared femoral versus internal jugular TCCs overall and within sequence strata. A registry-index cohort (patients with no documented prior TCC before January 2016, n = 135) was used to reduce, though not eliminate, sequence-related confounding in the site comparison; given only 24 CRBSI events, this analysis is exploratory and a clinically meaningful site difference cannot be excluded. Kaplan-Meier methods with log-rank testing were used for time-to-event outcomes. A cluster-robust marginal Cox model was used to account for repeated catheter insertions within patients, adjusting for sequence number, insertion site, age, sex, insertion setting, and exchange from a non-tunnelled catheter. RESULTS: Among 626 TCC insertions in 339 patients (389 FV, 237 IJV), contributing 98,727 catheter-days, CRBSI incidence escalated with catheter sequence: 1.17 per 1000 catheter-days for first insertions, rising to 1.98 for second and 2.49 for third-or-more insertions. Notably, by the second insertion, CRBSI rates were similar between FV and IJV access (31.7% each). In the index cohort (n = 135; FV = 95, IJV = 40), CRBSI-free survival did not differ significantly between sites (log-rank p = 0.340), nor did catheter survival (p = 0.950) or patient survival (p = 0.487). In the all-TCC cohort, after adjustment for catheter sequence number, age, sex, insertion setting, and exchange from a non-tunnelled catheter using a cluster-robust marginal Cox model, femoral access remained associated with a higher, though attenuated, CRBSI hazard after adjustment for the measured covariates (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.02-2.01; p = 0.039), indicating a modest residual site hazard beyond the sequence effect. CONCLUSIONS: Repeated catheterization was independently associated with increasing CRBSI risk, and catheter sequence number was the strongest predictor in the fully adjusted model. The femoral site effect was substantially attenuated after adjustment for sequence and was not statistically significant in the registry-index cohort analysis, though the wide confidence intervals preclude an equivalence interpretation. IJV access remains preferred; when IJV is unavailable, femoral TCC placement may be an acceptable alternative from an infection-risk perspective, but this must be weighed against thrombotic and limb complications, including deep vein thrombosis, which were not systematically ascertained in this study. Residual confounding cannot be excluded in this single-center retrospective study.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Tunnelled-cuffed catheters (TCCs) are widely used for haemodialysis access when permanent vascular access is unavailable. Internal jugular vein (IJV) placement is guideline-preferred, but femoral vein (FV) catheters are frequently used when upper venous access is limited. Whether femoral access confers a higher infection risk than catheter sequence number remains unclear.

title: Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes in patients with severe pelvic ring injury requiring REBOA: A two-center matched cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized. METHODS: This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up. Forty-nine REBOA-treated patients were matched 1:1 to 49 non-REBOA patients by major Young-Burgess category, Injury Severity Score, and age. The primary outcome was functional status among hospital survivors, categorized as good/fair/poor. Deep surgical site infection (SSI) after definitive pelvic fixation was the key secondary outcome, and nonunion was exploratory. Main models used a propensity-score linear predictor based on age, Injury Severity Score, initial systolic blood pressure, and lactate. RESULTS: Seventy-five patients survived hospitalization (30 REBOA; 45 non-REBOA); median follow-up was 19 months. Good/fair/poor outcomes were 16.7%/46.7%/36.7% in REBOA survivors and 51.1%/37.8%/11.1% in non-REBOA survivors. REBOA exposure was associated with worse functional status after adjustment (common odds ratio [cOR], 3.14; 95% CI, 1.11-8.92; P = 0.032). Among 68 definitive-fixation survivors, deep SSI occurred in 44.0% versus 9.3% (adjusted OR, 7.01; 95% CI, 1.88-31.07; P = 0.003); all observed events occurred within 60 days. Nonunion occurred in 26.7% versus 6.7% (adjusted OR, 9.09; 95% CI, 2.00-53.71; P = 0.004). Sensitivity analyses for deep SSI were directionally consistent. CONCLUSIONS: Among hospital survivors, REBOA exposure was associated with poorer long-term functional recovery and a higher burden of deep SSI. Nonunion was more frequent but remained exploratory. These findings characterize a high-risk orthopaedic survivor phenotype but do not establish a direct causal effect of REBOA.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized. METHODS: This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up.

title: The law of surprise: temporal variation and seasonality of acute aortic syndromes: a single-centre epidemiologic cohort analysis spanning 20 years.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Acute aortic syndromes (AAS) represent life-threatening cardiovascular emergencies characterized by high mortality rates despite rapid intervention. Global epidemiological data indicate substantial variance in incidence. Longitudinal single-centre data over extended periods are limited but crucial for understanding diagnostic, demographic, and systemic factors influencing admission trends.(1). This study aimed to analyze annual and seasonal variation trends of AAS over a 20-year period in a single maximal care centre and explore potential chronological and environmental contributors to this variation. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated 403 patients admitted with a confirmed diagnosis of AAS between 2005 and 2025 at the University Hospital Erlangen, Germany. All diagnoses were established via computed tomography angiography (CTA) and confirmed intraoperatively. Annual, quarterly, and monthly surgical volumes were calculated, and temporal trends were analyzed using Poisson and negative binomial regression models. Admission rates during public holidays and school vacations were also evaluated. RESULTS: Over the 20-year observation period, a steady increasing trend in the annual number of AAS cases was observed, peaking in 2017. Analysis of quarterly distributions revealed a statistically significant dominance of cases in the fourth quarter (Q4: October-December; p < 0.05) compared to the second (Q2) and third (Q3) quarters. Monthly analysis demonstrated a prominent peak in October (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.85 vs. June, p < 0.05). Conversely, fixed public holidays and school vacations were associated with statistically significant reductions in daily admission counts (p < 0.05), with the lowest relative case counts observed during the Christmas vacation period (IRR: 0.40-0.50). CONCLUSION: The case counts of acute aortic syndromes exhibits significant temporal and seasonal variation, characterized by a distinct late-autumn and early-winter peak, alongside significant declines during institutional vacation periods. These findings suggest that acute cardiovascular events are heavily modulated by cyclical environmental and socio-systemic factors.

title: Immunothrombosis Biomarkers and Multi-Omics Profiles After Successful Recanalization in Patients Receiving Ischemic Postconditioning: An Exploratory Analysis of the INSPIRE Trial.
abstract: Successful recanalization after endovascular thrombectomy does not always restore microvascular perfusion, highlighting the need for adjunctive strategies. Ischemic postconditioning (IPostC) involves brief, controlled​ cycles of flow interruption and restoration at the onset of reperfusion to attenuate ischemia-reperfusion injury. In the parent INSPIRE trial, IPostC, delivered in situ as four cycles of 2-minute balloon inflation followed by 2-minute deflation at the previously occluded arterial segment immediately after successful recanalization, reduced infarct growth from baseline to 48 h. This exploratory secondary analysis included all 60 randomized patients. We investigated whether IPostC was associated with early changes in immunothrombosis, coagulation, and microvascular transit and explored associated plasma proteomic and metabolomic profiles. Arterial blood obtained approximately 15 min after successful recanalization was analyzed using flow cytometry and thromboelastography. Quantitative digital subtraction angiography-derived microcirculation time was analyzed in 55 patients, and plasma proteomic and metabolomic profiling was performed in 29 patients. Compared with controls, patients receiving IPostC had lower neutrophil CD11b expression (median, 52.15 versus 64.27 mean fluorescence intensity ×10²; P = 0.011), a lower thromboelastography α-angle (65.15° versus 67.95°; P = 0.037), and shorter microcirculation time (2.11 versus 3.03 s; P = 0.020). Longer microcirculation time was associated with greater infarct growth (r = 0.533; P < 0.001). Proteomic and metabolomic analyses identified signals involving blood-brain barrier and extracellular-matrix organization and mitochondrial bioenergetics. Biomarker comparisons were not adjusted for multiple comparisons; in the omics analyses, no protein and 17 metabolites remained significant after false discovery rate correction. In summary, IPostC was associated with lower neutrophil activation, slower clot propagation, and faster microvascular transit after recanalization, and multi-omics profiling pointed to blood-brain barrier integrity and mitochondrial bioenergetics as candidate pathways. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger studies. Trial registration: NCT06545734, registered 9 August 2024.

Ischemic postconditioning (IPostC) involves brief, controlled​ cycles of flow interruption and restoration at the onset of reperfusion to attenuate ischemia-reperfusion injury. In the parent INSPIRE trial, IPostC, delivered in situ as four cycles of 2-minute balloon inflation followed by 2-minute deflation at the previously occluded arterial segment immediately after successful recanalization, reduced infarct growth from baseline to 48 h.
